1:
Gill and Ellicott both note where the chapter stands: after laws about the holiness of the people, the priests and the sacrifices come statutes about holy seasons. Henry makes the sequence a doctrine. Only God’s appointment can make time holy, since He is the Lord of time and sanctified one day above the rest as soon as the wheels were set going; a man may make a good day, but it is God’s prerogative to make a holy one, and as all inherent holiness comes from His special grace so all adherent holiness comes from His institution. He notices that they are called feasts although the day of atonement was a fast, and would rather render the word solemnities, which covers that day too. They were proclaimed, since they belonged not to the attending priests only but to all the people; and they were to be held as public assemblies, both because the institutions of God do not seek corners and their purity is best kept by open administration, and because the people are edified in love by meeting. Wesley adds that the proclaiming was done by the priests. Ellicott offers a closer rendering — the festivals of the Lord which ye shall proclaim as holy convocations, these are my festivals — taking the last clause as God claiming them for His own. Clarke works on the noun itself, which properly means any solemn anniversary by which great ecclesiastical or providential facts are recorded; such anniversaries were kept in every nation, and some became by regular observance the chronological epochs of history, as the Olympiads did.

The sabbath comes first, and they say why. Clarke calls it the first and greatest solemnity, and says roundly that whoever did not keep this in the most religious manner was incapable of keeping any of the others, since the religious observance of the sabbath stands at the very threshold of all religion. Ellicott makes it the oldest of the festivals and the one that recurs weekly, and reports the saying from the second Temple that the sabbath equals the whole law, so that whoever profanes it openly is as one who transgresses everything; its beginning and end, he adds, were announced by three blasts of the trumpet. Keil and Delitzsch place it at the head of the appointed seasons on a different ground: God had already sanctified it by His own rest on the seventh day of creation, and this is what distinguishes it from the yearly feasts, which commemorate the facts by which Israel was raised into a people of God. Gill notes only that the six days are days on which work may be done, any lawful work for a household’s sustenance.

Two of them independently press the same verbal distinction, and it carries real weight. Ellicott points out that the sabbath is forbidden any manner of work, whereas the other festivals in this chapter forbid only servile work and permit what is needed for preparing food; the sabbath and the day of atonement are the only days on which the Israelite might do nothing whatever. Wesley reaches the identical conclusion by reading the two formulas side by side: this manifest difference in the expressions used by the wise God must imply a difference in the things. Ellicott follows the rule into its later history: labour was punished by stoning, and the authorities registered minutely what counted as labour, yet ruled that in sickness and danger work is permitted, on the maxim that the sabbath is delivered into your hand and not you into the hand of the sabbath — which he compares with the declaration of Christ. Wesley draws a different corollary: the other feasts were to be kept before the Lord at Jerusalem, where all the males were to come, but the sabbath was to be kept everywhere, in the synagogues and in private houses alike.
4:
Ellicott explains why the heading is repeated: what follows are the festivals proper as distinguished from the weekly sabbath, proclaimed by trumpet blast on the appointed day. Wesley again prefers solemnities to feasts, for the reason Henry gave. Henry adds that they are the Lord’s because He appointed them, and contrasts the feast Jeroboam devised of his own heart. He then observes what months were chosen — roughly March, May and September — and why: not winter, when the days are short and the roads foul, and not high summer, when harvest and vintage could ill spare the people. God consults our comfort in what He appoints, which obliges us not to complain of His institutions as a burden. The solemnities were many and frequent, which kept Israel so employed that they had no leisure for the idolatrous neighbourhood around them; and they were mostly occasions of joy. Counting the days of strict rest, Henry finds six for holy joy and one for mourning, and draws the moral that we are commanded to rejoice evermore but not to be evermore weeping.

Keil and Delitzsch supply from the Hebrew what Ellicott and Wesley had argued from the English. Two distinct expressions are used: one means labour at a definite occupation, the work of a trade or calling, while the other covers any work at all, down to kindling a fire to cook with. On the sabbath and the day of atonement every kind of civil work was forbidden, even that; on the other festivals only the work of a calling. Ellicott fills in how this was administered later. Servile work was defined as building, weaving, reaping, threshing and grinding, while killing beasts, kneading dough, baking and roasting were permitted as needful; and the penalty differed, for the man who broke this rule was not stoned as a sabbath-breaker was, but given forty stripes save one.

Gill dates the passover by the month, Nisan or Abib, made first in the year because Israel came out of Egypt in it, and explains the next day as the one on which they went out carrying dough they had not had time to leaven. Calvin uses the passover to make a point about the commandments. He had treated its institution under the first commandment, because the rite initiated the people into God’s service and restrained them from the superstitions of the nations; but the day, recurring from year to year, belongs with the other festivals under the fourth, whose object was to exercise the people in the service of God. The killing of the lamb represented the grace of adoption, and its annual return kept Israel’s redemption perpetually in mind.

Ellicott supplies practical detail no one else has. The fourteenth falls about the beginning of April and was known both as the preparation for the passover and as its first day; on it every handicraftsman but the tailors, barbers and laundresses laid down work. Leaven might be eaten till midday and burnt in the afternoon, the moment signalled by two disqualified thank-offering cakes set out in the Temple, the first removed when eating must stop and the second when burning must begin. Every Israelite not infirm, defiled, uncircumcised or living beyond fifteen miles had to appear at Jerusalem with a gift proportioned to his means; country folk were lodged free by the townspeople and left their hosts the skins of the paschal lambs and the vessels they had used. He cites an eye-witness historian for the scale of it, some two and a half million people at one passover under Nero and a quarter of a million lambs killed, and concludes that most must have camped outside the walls as pilgrims still do at Mecca. He also records that on the intervening days the people gave themselves to dances, songs and games, and might water dry ground and repair watercourses and roads.
9:
Ellicott explains the fresh formula: the sheaf of firstfruits was no part of the original passover and could not have been observed in a wilderness where no corn was sown, so it is enacted prospectively, the third of four such laws in the book. He renders the offering not a sheaf but the firstfruit omer, and describes how it was gathered: the corn came from the best standing crop in a field near Jerusalem, delegates of the council tying the ears into bundles the day before while they were still rooted. What exactly was brought is disputed. Calvin argues for a handful placed in the priest’s hand rather than a measured tenth of an ephah, since a handful represents the beginning of harvest vividly; Wesley denies it was offered in the ear or by handful at all, citing an ancient historian for the claim that it was cleaned of chaff, dried and beaten out first.

Calvin makes the ceremony a defence against a particular error. The heathen invented gods presiding over the fruits until the earth became the mother of gods and men, and Israel would have fallen into that had this rite not reminded them that the Father of their subsistence is in heaven and the earth only His servant. Because the whole harvest was consecrated in a single handful, it was as though they confessed that everything the ground produced belonged to God; and His goodness appears in this, that in claiming His own He diminished nothing of the people’s food. He also distinguishes two Hebrew motions the English blurs, a lifting up and a waving toward the four quarters, and says the second is meant. Gill agrees the motion was to and fro and up and down, reports an authority who directs it eastward, taking its purpose to be an acknowledgment that the harvest came from the Lord. Clarke has the priest wave it before the people rather than before God, to call their attention to providence and stir their gratitude. Wesley has him wave it in the name of the whole congregation, which sanctified the rest of the harvest to them, and draws the lesson that we may eat our bread with joy only when God has accepted our works. Ellicott notes that the moment the rite was over the new bread and parched corn appeared for sale in Jerusalem, no use of the new crop being lawful until then.

The date of the waving was the sharpest question here. Ellicott reports that the phrase on the morrow after the sabbath divided the Pharisees from the Sadducees. The Pharisees took the word here, as elsewhere in this chapter, to mean not the weekly sabbath but the day of holy convocation that opened the feast, so that the omer was waved on the sixteenth; the Sadducees insisted on its literal sense, the ordinary sabbath falling somewhere inside the passover week. Ellicott decides for the Pharisees on a structural argument rather than a lexical one: since pentecost is counted from this day, a floating sabbath would leave pentecost without a fixed date and would in time displace the passover from its place in the year. Wesley takes the same view without mentioning the controversy, glossing the phrase as the day after the first day of unleavened bread and the first of the fifty that end at pentecost. On the doubled meat offering they divide again. Gill reports the Jewish account that one tenth belonged to the lamb and the other to the meat offering, and rejects it for a simpler reason, the plenty of the harvest, since thankfulness should be proportioned to mercies; Ellicott agrees, and Wesley adopts precisely the explanation Gill set aside. Gill adds that a man was beaten for eating so much as an olive’s bulk beforehand, and Clarke that parched and green ears, fried, are still eaten by the Arabs of the country.
15:
Ellicott corrects the rendering at once: seven sabbaths should be seven weeks, the word standing for a week here as in Deuteronomy and in the Greek of the New Testament, where the first day of the week is literally the first of the sabbath. Clarke gives the dates, from the sixteenth of the first month to the sixth of the third. Gill defends the starting point, insisting the sabbath meant is the first day of the feast and not the weekly one. Ellicott adds that Jews still begin the count at the close of the evening service on the second passover day.

Henry sets the two harvest feasts side by side. The sheaf of barley opened the harvest and gave liberty to put in the sickle; this feast solemnised its close. Then a handful of ears, now two wheaten loaves; then unleavened, in memory of the bread eaten at the exodus, now leavened, in acknowledgment of God’s goodness in their ordinary food; then a single lamb, now seven with two rams and a bullock, glorifying God as Lord of their land and harvest, together with a kid for a sin offering, by which they took shame to themselves as unworthy of the bread they ate. Keil and Delitzsch account for the enlargement by the meaning of the festival, a thanksgiving for the whole harvest rather than its firstfruits, and observe that where a private peace offering left most of the flesh to the offerer, here it fell to the priest. Wesley explains that differently: the whole congregation being the offerer, the portion could not be divided among all nor given to some without offence.

The list of victims does not agree with the list in Numbers, and two of them face it. Ellicott, following the second-Temple authorities, makes the two passages describe distinct sets of sacrifices, those in Numbers appointed for the wilderness and these only after the entry into the land. Wesley offers either a liberty of choice, or a division by which one bullock and one ram belonged to the feast day while the others attended the loaves — from which he draws the rule that a new sacrifice never cancelled an old one. Gill reports a rabbinic dispute about the waving, whether the lambs were held above the bread or the bread above the lambs, and a proposed reconciliation that the bread was laid alongside. Wesley thinks only a part was waved for the whole; Ellicott describes the full ceremony: the living lambs waved and then killed, the breast and shoulder laid beside the loaves and moved eastward and up and down, the fat burnt and the rest eaten by the priests.

Ellicott records what the day became: the authorities of the second Temple took it for the anniversary of the giving of the Decalogue, and that commemoration has since displaced its harvest character, the feast being kept with houses and synagogues dressed in flowers. Wesley reaches the same association independently, making the feast a memorial both of the law given on the fiftieth day and of the progress of harvest, and adds what he calls its perfection, the outpouring of the Spirit on the apostles that same day, fifty days after Christ our passover was sacrificed, when three thousand souls became the firstfruits of the Christian church. On the closing command about the corners and gleanings, Keil and Delitzsch see the point of its placement: thanksgiving for harvest was not enough unless the poor were remembered in the reaping. Gill rejects the rabbinic saying that whoever leaves them is as one who built the sanctuary, and gives a better reason, that thankfulness should be attended by liberality to men. Wesley notices the change from plural to singular, pressing the duty on every individual who has a harvest, and concludes that devotion to God is little esteemed unless accompanied by acts of charity.
23:
All of them make this in effect a new year’s day. Henry notes that the seventh month had once been reckoned the first and that the jubilee still began with it; Clarke says the feast probably had no other design than to mark the opening of the civil year; Ellicott confirms that it has been called the Festival of New Year ever since the second Temple. Wesley gives it a second purpose: as the seventh day was a sabbath and the seventh year a sabbatical year, God would have the seventh month a kind of sabbatical month, and the trumpets at its opening were to quicken the people for the sabbaths it contained. On the blowing itself, Henry and Wesley agree that although a trumpet was sounded at every new moon, this one was done with special solemnity, from sunrise until sunset; Wesley adds that it was heard not in Jerusalem only but in every city, and Gill that the obligation to hear bound priests, Levites, Israelites, proselytes and freedmen, though not bondservants, women or children, and that nine distinct soundings had to be heard.

What the trumpets were a memorial of nobody can settle. Henry offers the trumpet at Sinai when the law was given, then reports the view that it commemorated the creation of the world, supposed to have taken place in autumn, which is why this had been the first month; and he finds that fitting, since the word by which God made the world is called the voice of His thunder and the sons of God shouted for joy when the foundations were fastened — the Aramaic version rendering the phrase a memorial of shouting. Clarke passes on the same suggestion about creation without adopting it. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as remembrance blowing and takes it to mean that the trumpets summoned Israel into the work of sanctification, for which they would be remembered before the Lord; but he adds that the synagogue understands the remembering the other way, as reminding God of the merits of the patriarchs and of His covenant with them, which is why the lessons appointed for the day are those recording the birth and the binding of Isaac.

Calvin attacks that reading with unusual heat. He wonders how it ever entered the mind of the Jews that the feast commemorated the deliverance of Isaac and the beast substituted for him, and says they invented it with their accustomed audacity, calling it as baseless as it is unreasonable. Others do better, he allows, in taking the day as a preparation for the atonement, since the interval is short and this day carries no mark of its own. But he prefers a third account: that they were called together once a year by trumpet so that they might learn that all their sacred assemblies were appointed by the voice of God, and that this voice was renewed among them to keep them always ready to obey. Ellicott, without argument, agrees that the day was regarded as preparatory to the atonement ten days later.

Gill limits the prohibited work to what a servant would do, allowing what was needed to dress food; Ellicott says all handicraft and trade stopped except what was necessary. Ellicott alone describes the day’s service. Since the festival was also a new moon, three sacrifices were offered in succession, the daily one first, then the monthly, then the offering proper to the feast, which differed from the monthly only in having one bullock instead of two. While the offerings were made the Levites sang and played, and at intervals the priests broke in with blasts of the trumpets; the service closed with the benediction, received prostrate, after which the congregation went to the synagogue for the appointed lessons and for prayers that the past year’s sins might be pardoned and the new one be happy.
26:
Gill observes that the introductory formula marks off one precept from another, and explains why it was omitted before pentecost: that feast depended on the wave sheaf and was reckoned from it. Calvin begins with the word itself, which means both to propitiate and to blot out guilt by expiation, and stands here in the plural because Israel was not under one kind of guilt but needed manifold reconciliations. Such expiation went on through the year, every victim being a satisfaction offered to obtain pardon; but a yearly day was added as a special memorial and a sharper spur to repentance, because a people who had provoked God’s anger for twelve months needed stirring to pious grief. On this day they were cited before God’s tribunal, to stand there acknowledging that they deserved the judgment while praying to escape the punishment; and meanwhile the sacrifices taught them that they were restored to favour, since bare confession would have left only a ground for despair. Keil and Delitzsch describe the observance plainly: a holy meeting, a fast from the evening of the ninth until the evening of the tenth, rest from all work on pain of death, and sacrifices.

What it meant to afflict the soul is agreed to be fasting, but the voices attach different weight to it. Wesley adds bitter repentance for their national sins, among which he thinks God would have them remember the golden calf, since He had threatened to remember it in order to punish, and they had the more reason to remember it in order to humble themselves. Gill records that the ancient versions read the threat as aimed at one who can fast and does not, a sick person and a child under nine being exempt; Ellicott states the same exemption for age and sickness. Calvin turns the penalty into a doctrine. That God should punish contempt of this ceremony so severely shows how greatly the sacrifice of a humbled heart pleases Him; and to rest secure in luxuries at the very moment God is inspiring dread of His wrath and inviting tears would be gross indifference. He recalls the oath in Isaiah against those who, called to weeping and sackcloth, feasted instead and said let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. So long as a sinner is pricked enough to sigh for a remedy there is hope of recovery; the man who has shaken off fear along with shame is altogether desperate. Wesley reads the same threat as signifying the absolute necessity every man has of repentance and forgiveness, and the desperate condition of the impenitent.

Ellicott works over the wording. This is the only day besides the sabbath on which no manner of work was permitted; and where every other threat of excision uses cut off, here the word is destroy, a stronger term he attributes to the day’s solemnity — though he notes the curious result that labour on the sabbath was punished by stoning while labour on this day was punished only by excision. The command against work is repeated after the penalty to press it home, and the command to fast after that, lest anyone suppose keeping half the law would answer for the whole. He also twice faults the translators for varying an English formula where the Hebrew does not. Gill makes the same point about the repetition, that it shows how strictly God required the day to be kept. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as resting your rest, the rest binding on them from all laborious work. Wesley notices that this one is called your sabbath where the weekly one is often called the sabbath of the Lord, and closes with an observation of his own: the Jews begin each day at evening in remembrance of creation, while Christians generally begin theirs with the morning in memory of the resurrection.
33:
Henry makes much of where the feast falls, five days after the fast: the afflicting of their souls on the day of atonement prepared them for this joy, since the more we are humbled for sin the better qualified we are for comfort. It was, he adds, the most joyful of the pilgrim feasts. Calvin gives the reason the chapter supplies at its close, that they might remember dwelling in tents in the desert, and contrasts it with the passover: that showed how they were rescued from death, while this magnifies the continuous flow of grace, since it would not be enough to thank God for a momentary deliverance without reflecting on the whole forty years. He notices that Zechariah, foretelling a second redemption, requires the converted nations to keep this feast in particular, and explains the choice by the return from Babylon being as memorable as the exodus; though the ceremony is abolished, its use survives in spirit and in truth. Wesley adds that they were to bless God for the protection given then and the settled dwellings now.

Over the word for the closing day, Calvin and Keil and Delitzsch part company. Calvin observes that it derives from a root meaning both to restrain and to gather, that some render it the prohibition of God, and that he prefers to take it as a solemnity, leaving his readers to choose. Keil and Delitzsch allow neither: the word means the solemn close of a festival lasting several days, from the sense of shutting in, and is derived neither from gathering the people nor from the prohibition of work. Wesley argues that the eighth day, though not one of the seven, is the great day of the feast in the Gospel, the removal from booths into houses figuring the settlement in Canaan.

Ellicott points out that the law prescribes neither how nor where the booths were to be built, the details being left to those administering it. He supplies them from later practice: after the exile they were made on roofs, in courtyards and in the streets, of olive, myrtle and palm branches; and the rabbis fixed that a booth must have three walls and a roof left partly open to the sky, must not stand under a tree, and must be roofed only with what grows out of the ground. Clarke turns to pagan parallels, reporting that the Gentiles had feasts of tents of their own; he cites an ancient writer who inferred from this very custom that the Jews worshipped Bacchus, whose vintage festival was likewise called the feast of tabernacles and kept with tents of vine branches and ivy.

Ellicott alone records the temple ceremonies. At daybreak a priest went with a golden pitcher to Siloam and returned through the water-gate to three trumpet blasts, mounting the altar with another priest carrying wine, and the two poured water and wine into pierced silver basins so that both emptied together at its base; another company set willows about it so that their tops formed a canopy. At night four golden candelabra were lit in the court, throwing light over the whole city, and men danced with torches while the Levites played from the fifteen steps answering to the psalms of degrees; and on the last evening, as that illumination was about to be put out, Ellicott supposes Christ called attention to himself. Calvin ends on the caution against diminishing the ordinary service, lest they transfer to the feast days sacrifices already owed and so, as the saying is, whitewash two walls out of the same pot. Ellicott makes the same point from a figure of speech: sabbaths stands for the sacrifices of the sabbaths, so a festival falling on a sabbath does not cancel them. Gill and Wesley agree, Wesley adding that these are called the sabbaths of the Lord in contrast with festival days sometimes so named.
39:
Ellicott explains the return to a feast already legislated: after the list has been summed up, these verses come back to tabernacles with supplementary regulations forming a separate enactment. Wesley says the same, that this is no new law but a repetition with a fuller explanation, and defines the ingathering precisely — not the corn, gathered long before, but the fruit of the vines and olives, which completed the year’s harvest. Ellicott adds that this is why the feast bears the further name of the ingathering.

What the goodly trees are, nobody agrees. Gill reports that the ancient Aramaic versions understand citrons, and that Jews in countries where the fruit does not grow will send to Spain for it; the bundle must also be the worshipper’s own property, though a gift will serve even if given on condition of return. Clarke likewise reports the citron, and takes the thick trees for myrtle. Ellicott shows how the identification was reached: the phrase might mean the fruit of any choice tree, so the lawgiver left it to those administering the law, who fastened on a sense of the word meaning to rest and decided it must be the fruit that stays permanently on the tree, the citron — illegal if it came from an uncircumcised tree or showed the slightest blemish. Calvin refuses the whole procedure: some take the word for a proper name, but since it everywhere means comeliness he is unwilling to depart from its ordinary sense. Wesley identifies the trees differently, from the first celebration after the exile: olive, myrtle and pine, the most plentiful in the country and the best at keeping their greenness, with willows to bind them; and the same branches, he notes, were both built into the booths and carried in the hand.

Calvin reads the branches as a signal that the day was to be kept with gladness. It was a memorial of the favour shown their fathers in the desert, exposed to every vicissitude of the weather while God cherished them as an eagle does her brood, and also a thanksgiving for the reception since given them in the land; it would have been unreasonable to enter the booths in sorrow when they set before the eye both the former and the present goodness of God, and gave a foretaste of heaven to men still only sojourners. Clarke finds two objects in the institution: to perpetuate the memory of the deliverance from Egypt and the preservation in the wilderness, and to keep alive gratitude and obedience. Since we deserve nothing at God’s hands and gratitude is the only debt we can pay, he says, we should pay it cheerfully and often; an ungrateful heart is an unfeeling, unloving, unbelieving and disobedient heart. Ellicott puts it soberly: when their descendants were securely settled in the land, a week under branches once a year would remind them how their fathers had been sheltered.

Wesley notes that the booths were put up in the towns, in streets and gardens and on the flat roofs of houses. Gill and Ellicott agree the obligation ran seven days only, the eighth being a separate festival when the booths were left; and Gill records that the Jewish writers would not go out until they had dined there, praying as they left that they might be worthy the next year to dwell in the booth of Leviathan — that is, to feast with the Messiah — and that a ninth day was later added for joy at the completed reading of the law. Ellicott closes the chapter as it began, with Moses explaining the number and motive of these festivals. Wesley closes with a comparison: we have reason to be thankful that our feasts are neither so many nor so costly, but more spiritual and significant, and sweeter earnests of the everlasting feast at the last ingathering.
